title: Materials Science for Engineers
description: Materials Science for Engineers connects atomic structure, microstructure, and processing to mechanical and functional properties. Students learn bonding, crystals, defects, diffusion, stress-strain behavior, phase diagrams and heat treatment, failure modes, major material families, materials selection, and manufacturing with sustainability.

topics.title: Atomic Structure and Bonding
topics.description: Materials behavior begins at the atomic scale. This topic explains how electrons, bonds, and atomic arrangements shape stiffness, melting temperature, conductivity, and chemical stability.

children.title: Atomic structure
children.description: Students learn how atomic number, electron configuration, and valence influence material behavior.

children.title: Primary bonding
children.description: Primary bonds explain why materials differ so strongly in stiffness, melting point, and electrical behavior.

children.title: Secondary bonding
children.description: Secondary bonds help explain polymers, molecular solids, and many surface or interface phenomena.

children.title: Bonding-property links
children.description: Students connect atomic-scale bonding to engineering-scale material properties.

topics.title: Crystal Structures
topics.description: Crystal structure describes how atoms are arranged in solids. It controls density, slip, anisotropy, diffusion paths, and many mechanical and physical properties.

children.title: Unit cells and lattices
children.description: Students learn the repeating geometric building blocks of crystalline materials.

children.title: Common metallic structures
children.description: FCC, BCC, and HCP structures explain many differences in ductility, strength, and deformation behavior.

children.title: Crystallographic directions and planes
children.description: Directions and planes provide the language for slip, diffraction, and anisotropy.

children.title: Noncrystalline and semicrystalline structures
children.description: Not all materials are perfectly crystalline, so students learn amorphous and mixed structures.

topics.title: Imperfections and Defects
topics.description: Real materials are not perfect crystals. Defects often determine strength, ductility, conductivity, diffusion, and failure.

children.title: Point defects
children.description: Point defects change local chemistry and enable diffusion and property control.

children.title: Line defects
children.description: Dislocations explain plastic deformation and strengthening in crystalline solids.

children.title: Planar defects
children.description: Interfaces and boundaries strongly affect mechanical and thermal behavior.

children.title: Defects and properties
children.description: Students learn that defects can be harmful, useful, or deliberately engineered.

children.title: Defect effects on conductivity and corrosion

topics.title: Diffusion in Solids
topics.description: Diffusion is atomic movement through solids. It controls heat treatment, carburizing, sintering, creep, oxidation, and many manufacturing processes.

children.title: Diffusion mechanisms
children.description: Students learn how atoms move through crystals and why defects matter.

children.title: Fick's laws
children.description: Fick's laws turn diffusion into a quantitative engineering model.

children.title: Temperature dependence
children.description: Diffusion is strongly temperature-dependent, which explains why heat treatment and processing schedules matter.

children.title: Engineering applications
children.description: Students connect diffusion to practical materials processing and degradation.

topics.title: Mechanical Properties (Stress-Strain)
topics.description: Mechanical properties describe how materials respond to load. This topic teaches students to read stress-strain curves and use mechanical data in design.

children.title: Elastic behavior
children.description: Elastic behavior captures reversible deformation and stiffness.

children.title: Plastic deformation
children.description: Plasticity describes permanent deformation and is central to forming, yielding, and ductility.

children.title: Strength and toughness
children.description: Strength and toughness describe different aspects of load capacity and damage tolerance.

children.title: Testing and data interpretation
children.description: Students learn where property values come from and how to interpret them critically.

topics.title: Phase Diagrams
topics.description: Phase diagrams map stable phases as composition and temperature change. They are essential for understanding alloys, heat treatment, solidification, and microstructure.

children.title: Phase rule and equilibrium
children.description: Students learn the logic behind phase stability and how many variables can be controlled independently.

children.title: Binary phase diagrams
children.description: Binary diagrams are the workhorse for alloy interpretation.

children.title: Lever rule
children.description: The lever rule lets students estimate phase fractions from a diagram.

children.title: Iron-carbon diagram
children.description: The iron-carbon system is a major engineering example because it underlies steel heat treatment.

topics.title: Phase Transformations and Heat Treatment
topics.description: Phase transformations let engineers change microstructure and properties through controlled processing.

children.title: Nucleation and growth
children.description: Students learn the mechanism by which new phases form and grow.

children.title: Time-temperature-transformation behavior
children.description: Transformation diagrams connect temperature histories to microstructures.

children.title: Steel heat treatment
children.description: Heat treatment of steel demonstrates how processing creates useful property combinations.

children.title: Precipitation and age hardening
children.description: Some alloys strengthen through controlled precipitation rather than simple phase conversion.

topics.title: Failure (Fracture, Fatigue, Creep)
topics.description: Materials fail in different ways depending on stress, defects, temperature, time, and environment. This topic teaches students to recognize and prevent common failure modes.

children.title: Fracture
children.description: Fracture mechanics links cracks, stress, and material toughness.

children.title: Fatigue
children.description: Fatigue explains failure under repeated loading below static strength.

children.title: Creep
children.description: Creep is time-dependent deformation at elevated temperature.

children.title: Failure analysis
children.description: Students learn to infer causes from evidence rather than treating failure as a single event.

topics.title: Metals and Alloys
topics.description: Metals and alloys are central engineering materials because they combine strength, ductility, conductivity, processability, and recyclability.

children.title: Ferrous alloys
children.description: Steels and cast irons show how composition and heat treatment tailor properties.

children.title: Nonferrous alloys
children.description: Nonferrous metals serve needs where weight, corrosion, conductivity, or temperature resistance dominate.

children.title: Strengthening mechanisms
children.description: Students learn how alloy design and processing increase strength.

children.title: Corrosion and protection
children.description: Metals interact with their environment, so corrosion prevention is part of material selection.

topics.title: Polymers, Ceramics, and Composites
topics.description: These major material families broaden design options beyond metals. Students learn how structure and processing create very different property profiles.

children.title: Polymers
children.description: Polymers offer low density, processability, and tunable mechanical/thermal behavior.

children.title: Ceramics
children.description: Ceramics offer hardness, heat resistance, and chemical stability but are often brittle.

children.title: Composites
children.description: Composites combine phases to achieve properties not available from one material alone.

children.title: Family-level tradeoffs
children.description: Students learn to compare material families by function, manufacturing, environment, and cost.

topics.title: Materials Selection and Design
topics.description: This added synthesis topic turns materials science into engineering choice: selecting materials that satisfy function, constraints, cost, reliability, and manufacturability.

children.title: Selection criteria
children.description: Students learn to translate design needs into material property requirements.

children.title: Materials property charts
children.description: Property charts help compare many materials visually and quantitatively.

children.title: Design indices
children.description: Design indices connect performance objectives to material properties.

children.title: Data and databases
children.description: Students learn to use material data sources responsibly.

children.title: Uncertainty, test conditions, and datasheet limits

topics.title: Processing, Manufacturing, and Sustainability
topics.description: This added topic connects structure and properties to how materials are made, shaped, inspected, and used responsibly over a product life cycle.

children.title: Processing-structure-property relationships
children.description: Students learn that manufacturing processes change microstructure, and microstructure changes properties.

children.title: Manufacturing process constraints
children.description: Material choice must fit realistic process capability, tolerances, and cost.

children.title: Quality and characterization
children.description: Testing and inspection verify that material and processing choices achieved the intended properties.

children.title: Sustainable materials thinking
children.description: Students consider environmental and life-cycle impacts alongside performance.
